name: Hair cloning

card.summary: Multiplying follicle cells in a lab to grow unlimited hair is a long-promised idea that remains in animal and lab research.
card.note: No approved product; commercial programmes have closed.

quick.overview:
Hair cloning would take cells from healthy follicles, multiply them in culture, and implant them to make new hair follicles, avoiding the donor limits of transplantation.

Per Wikipedia, it is in early stages, with milestones in mice and several company programmes ended.
quick.mechanism: Follicle-inducing cells such as dermal papilla cells, or iPSC-derived cells, are expanded in the lab and implanted to interact with scalp epithelium and form follicles.
quick.risks: No approved treatment exists, so no human safety record is cited. Obstacles listed include inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles and cycling shown only in mice.

lead: Hair cloning, also called hair multiplication or follicle neogenesis, is a proposed regenerative approach to hair loss. Cells from healthy follicles, such as dermal papilla cells, are multiplied in the laboratory and implanted into thinning or bald scalp, where they are meant to induce new follicles [1][2]. The look it is aiming at is a fuller head of hair, including a restored hairline and crown, without being limited by how much donor hair a person has.

That limit is the central constraint of hair transplantation, which relocates existing follicles from the back and sides of the scalp. A cloning approach would in principle turn a small sample into many follicles, which is why people with extensive hair loss, limited donor hair or hair loss at a young age follow the field closely [1][2][10].

The idea has a research history of roughly two decades. A 2005 review described follicular cell implantation as an emerging therapy [10], companies including Intercytex and Aderans ran programmes that ended in 2008 and 2013 [2], and academic groups have since reported hair grown from engineered cells in mice, including from induced pluripotent stem cells [2][12][13]. As of the sources consulted, no human-cloned-follicle treatment is approved and the results are in laboratory and animal models; Stemson Therapeutics closed in December 2024 and a February 2026 RIKEN and OrganTech report described engineered follicles that cycled for 68 days in mice [2].

chain: Take cells from a small scalp sample
Multiply follicle-inducing cells in the lab
Implant them into thinning or bald scalp
New follicles and fuller hair without donor-supply limits
angle.text: The intended payoff is hair density where a person has little: new follicles grown from a few cultured cells, for hairlines and crowns that transplantation cannot fully cover. So far, parts of the process have been shown in mice and in the laboratory.

paras: Proposed methods take dermal papilla cells or follicle stem cells from a small scalp sample, expand them in culture, and implant them where they are meant to induce new follicles through interaction with surrounding epithelial cells [1]. Newer lines of work use induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) made from patient cells, 3D cell aggregates and scaffolds, including 3D-printed biodegradable shafts [1][2][3].

Compared with hair transplantation, a cloning approach would aim to produce additional follicles from a small cell sample, so the number of grafts available would no longer be set by the donor area [1][2]. A related line of research studies wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis, in which full-thickness wounds in adult mammals regenerate new follicles; reviews describe the signalling pathways involved and the process as similar to embryonic development [4][5].

sections.h: The rationale: what bald scalp lacks
paras: Earlier assumptions held that completely bald scalp has lost its follicles. Wikipedia describes a 2012 University of Pennsylvania finding that bald and non-bald scalp contain similar numbers of stem cells but that progenitor cells are depleted in bald areas, which points to failed activation rather than absence of stem cells [2]. A 2013 review by Chueh and colleagues cites the same line of work and notes that in androgenetic alopecia the hair stem cells appear normal while activation to form hair germs is defective [11].

The same review describes dermal papilla cells from balding scalp as having higher androgen receptor levels and 5-alpha-reductase activity, with DHT prompting them to release factors that inhibit keratinocyte growth, and the papillae shrinking and becoming senescent [11]. Cell-based therapy therefore faces a practical problem the review states directly: dermal papilla cells grow slowly in culture and quickly lose their hair-inducing ability [11].

Teumer and Cooley's 2005 review in Seminars in Plastic Surgery set out the concept: a few donor dermal papilla cells are expanded in culture and implanted into the scalp to form many new follicles. They proposed using androgen-insensitive donor cells from the donor area, discussed culture systems using keratinocyte co-culture and WNT signalling that kept cells inductive, and noted that no quantitative studies had established the minimum number of cells needed to form a hair [10]. They also argued dermal papilla and sheath cells might be transplantable between people without acute rejection, citing a single human case of male donor cells in a female recipient with new hair at 3 to 5 weeks and no rejection signs to 11 weeks [10]. The authors expected the therapy might become available in the coming years; the review reports no controlled human trial data [10].

According to Wikipedia, Intercytex in the UK worked on follicle cloning from cells taken from the back of the neck and concluded in 2008 that it had not fully developed its therapy [2]. In 2010 researchers at Technische Universität Berlin, with Intercytex and others, produced follicles from animal cells that were thinner than normal [2]. Aderans Research Institute in Japan, with a process Wikipedia calls Ji Gami that removes a strip of scalp and culture-expands follicular cells before reinjection, ran trials into 2012 and ended funding in July 2013; Wikipedia flags that passage as needing better sourcing [2].

sections.h: Stem-cell and organ-germ milestones in mice (2013 to 2026)
paras: A 2013 review by Chueh and colleagues grouped strategies for hair regeneration into hair cycle activation, niche modulation, wound-induced follicle neogenesis and stem cell engineering, and proposed expanding dermal papilla cells as aggregates, since aggregates better preserve inductive ability [11]. A 2014 review of emerging alopecia treatments also discusses cell-based approaches [7]. In 2015, according to Wikipedia, early trials generated new human-derived follicles in mice whose hairs grew in varying directions [2].

In 2016 a Japanese group led by Takashi Tsuji, with first author Ryoji Takagi, reported in Science Advances that clusters of embryoid bodies from mouse iPSCs, transplanted under the kidney capsule of immunodeficient mice, formed skin-like tissue with hair follicles; Wnt10b signalling increased follicle number. When grafted onto nude mouse skin the follicles grew hair in about 14 days, connected to host muscle and nerve fibres, and cycled at least three times over 90 days, with no tumours in 3 months [12]. Wikipedia lists the group's partnership with Organ Technologies, Kyocera and RIKEN [2]. A separate 2016 laboratory study generated iPSCs from human hair follicle keratinocytes as a possible source for follicle cloning [3].

In July 2019 Stemson Therapeutics (San Diego) and UC San Diego reported follicles in mice from iPSC-derived epithelial and dermal cells, with hair aligned using a 3D-printed biodegradable shaft [2]. In October 2022 Yokohama National University researchers led by Tatsuto Kageyama and Junji Fukuda published in Science Advances a method using mouse embryonic skin cells in Matrigel aggregates that raised hair-shaft sprouting from under 1 percent to nearly 100 percent of aggregates; shafts reached about 3 mm by day 23, though the model used rodent cells and the in vitro follicles regressed within about a month, whereas transplanted aggregates cycled for at least 10 months [13]. In February 2026 Wikipedia records a RIKEN and OrganTech report led by Tsuji identifying a third key cell type, dermal condensate mesenchymal cells, with engineered follicles producing 3 mm shafts that cycled for 68 days in mice [2].

Hair follicle development depends on signalling between epithelial cells and dermal papilla cells. A 2025 review of Wnt10b reports that this signal promotes hair morphogenesis by inducing the dermal papilla in the embryo, governs the fate of hair follicle stem cells, and coordinates them with melanocyte stem cells to regenerate pigmented hair [8]. Reviews of wound-induced follicle neogenesis describe an embryonic-like regenerative phenomenon in adult mammals [4][5]. A 2021 mouse study reported that wound-induced follicle neogenesis and stem cell markers correlated with skin bacterial counts, being lowest in germ-free mice [6]. A 2025 review of retinoids in scarless skin regeneration notes their potential to modulate wound repair, including reconstitution of hair follicles and other appendages [9].

No published studies in humans demonstrate hair cloning as a treatment. Related work is laboratory and animal research: iPSC and organ-germ studies in mice [3][12][13], wound-induced follicle neogenesis in mice [4][5][6], and review literature [7][10][11].

Wikipedia lists inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles in earlier methods, depleted progenitor cells in bald scalp, and cycling shown only in mice as open problems, along with the closure or funding end of several commercial programmes [2]. Reviews add the slow growth and loss of inductive ability of cultured dermal papilla cells, the need to place cells at the right depth, angle and number, immune tolerance questions for donor cells, and producing thousands of follicles per patient [10][11]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes related stem-cell injection results as modest and inconsistent [1].

Hair cloning periodically appears in news coverage and hair-loss discussion as a prospective cure for baldness, and the closures of company programmes and long timelines are part of that conversation [2]. In the meantime, people with hair loss use approved medications, hair transplantation or cosmetic coverings, which are covered in other articles.

timeline.event: Teumer and Cooley publish a review describing follicular cell implantation as an emerging therapy.[10]
Intercytex concludes its follicle therapy is not fully developed.[2]
Follicles grown from animal cells with Intercytex involvement are thinner than normal.[2]
University of Pennsylvania reports depleted progenitor cells, not missing stem cells, in bald scalp.[2]
Aderans stops funding hair multiplication research; Chueh and colleagues publish a review of regeneration strategies.[2][11]
Takagi, Tsuji and colleagues grow hair-bearing skin organ from iPSCs in mice; iPSC study from human follicle keratinocytes published.[3][12]
Stemson Therapeutics and UC San Diego report follicles in mice from iPSC-derived cells.[2]
Yokohama National University reports hair-shaft sprouting in near 100 percent of mouse cell aggregates.[13]
RIKEN and OrganTech report dermal condensate cells and follicles cycling for 68 days in mice.[2]
